newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentina and Britain hold new round of oil talks.
newsitem.headline: Argentina and Britain hold new round of oil talks.

text.p: British and Argentine officials began three days of talks in Buenos Aires on Monday on oil exploration around the disputed Falkland Islands and how to set up joint ventures and protect the environment.

The two-nation South West Atlantic Hydrocarbons Commission last met in London in December, when it agreed a timetable for a joint round of oil licensing for a "Special Cooperation Zone" southwest of the islands.

The government of the British-run islands in the South Atlantic, where Britain and Argentina fought a 10-week war in 1982, awarded permits for exploration in waters close to the islands to 12 companies last October.
Britain and Argentina must now hold a joint tender before year-end for licenses for the Special Cooperation Area which straddles the line between the islands and the Argentine mainland.

Diplomats from both countries told Reuters there would be no comment on the talks until after they end on Wednesday, apart from a statement issued by the Argentine Foreign Ministry which said they "continue analysing the technical aspects of the call for a tender in the special cooperation area."

It said the talks would look at "recommendations...for the protection of the marine environment, promoting cooperation by industry from both sides including setting up joint ventures and elaborating joint projects in exploration, production and the use of infrastructure."
The talks are taking place under a so-called "diplomatic umbrella" by which both sides agree to put aside sovereignty claims and tackle specific issues such as oil and fishing.

Argentina lost the 1982 war for the islands it calls the Malvinas but continues to press its 150-year-old territorial claim. However both countries resumed diplomatic links in 1989 and signed an agreement on oil and gas exploration in 1995.
The complex accord allows each country to levy royalties -- the Falklands nine percent and Argentina three percent -- without recognising each other's right to levy the charge.
